clue.text: Relative partly installs fruit machine that talks?

indicators.note: to install something is to put it inside, so the shortened relative goes around the fruit
only part of the relative is used, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: an aunt is a relative
botanically a tomato is a fruit

explanation.surface: A relative fits a fruit machine with a gadget that speaks, a seaside arcade novelty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit machine' looks like one unit, a British slot machine, but the two words split between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An automaton is a mechanical figure built to imitate a person, and the question mark admits that not every such robot actually speaks.

clue.text: Section of mounted slide bore a nasty bug?

indicators.note: in a down entry, mounted means going upward, so the run is read from bottom to top
a section is a run of letters lifted straight out of the following words

parts.note: the letters of these words, read backwards, contain the answer

explanation.surface: A nasty germ seen on a microscope slide mounted for viewing.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'sliDE BORE ANAsty' backwards: Y-T-S-A-N-A-E-R-O-B-E-D-I-L-S holds ANAEROBE. 'Mounted slide' sounds like lab equipment, but 'mounted' is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An anaerobe is a microorganism that lives without oxygen, and bug is the informal word for such a germ.

clue.text: Claw oddly scratched floor coated with bronze

indicators.note: a coating wraps all round, so the colour word goes outside the kept letters

parts.note: tan is a bronze, sunburnt colour

indicators.note: scratching out the odd-numbered letters leaves only the even ones

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of floor

explanation.surface: A bronze floor scratched by some creature's claw.
explanation.definitionFit: A talon is the hooked claw of a bird of prey.

clue.text: Female crosses further down: bear doesn't follow

indicators.note: a woman who crosses something here spans it from one side to the other, holding it within her

parts.note: Miss is the title for an unmarried woman
under means lower down
to stand something is to bear or tolerate it

explanation.surface: A woman crossing further down the slope while a bear is not trailing behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon suggests the bear explains the woman's route; in fact the definition sits after it.
explanation.definitionFit: If you misunderstand someone you fail to grasp their meaning, just as you cannot follow an argument you do not get.

clue.text: Drum in time with game old doctors travelling north

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time

indicators.note: in a down entry, moving north means reading upward, so the group is turned round

parts.note: RU is Rugby Union
O is the abbreviation for old
the BMA, British Medical Association, is the doctors' professional body

explanation.surface: A drumbeat keeping time with a game played by old doctors on the move.
explanation.walkthrough: T, then RU + O + BMA turned upward. The BMA is the trade body for British doctors.
explanation.definitionFit: A tambour is a small drum, the old word behind tambourine.

clue.text: Saw clumsily into 50% of trees

indicators.note: something done clumsily is botched and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: fifty per cent means half, so the back half of the word is dropped

parts.note: cedars are trees

explanation.surface: Someone sawed clumsily into half the trees in a wood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trees' stands for CEDARS, half of which is CED. 'Saw' looks like the cutting tool in this woodland scene, but it is the past tense of see.
explanation.definitionFit: To have noticed something is to have seen or spotted it, so the past tense of see fits.

clue.text: Heroic tale of half perhaps fleeing outbreak

indicators.note: what flees runs away, so that part leaves the longer word

parts.note: an epidemic is an outbreak of disease
demi- is a prefix meaning half

explanation.surface: A heroic tale of half the population fleeing an outbreak of plague.
explanation.walkthrough: EPIDEMIC without DEMI leaves EPI + C.
explanation.definitionFit: An epic is a long narrative poem celebrating the deeds of heroes, like the Iliad.

clue.text: Horrid wearing stuffed shirt close to fire, right?

indicators.note: a word wearing another has it on like clothing, so the shirt goes around the nasty word

parts.note: a stuffed shirt is a pompous, self-righteous person
vile means horrid

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its last letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter of fire

explanation.surface: A horrid pompous figure warming himself close to the fire, as is his due.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right?' reads like a tag question, but it is the definition, a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A privilege is a special right or advantage granted to some and not others.

clue.text: Fruit drink primarily avoided after cold

indicators.note: the primary letter is the first, and it is avoided, so it drops off
after places the shortened drink behind the cold letter in the answer

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
sherry is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: A fruit drink skipped in favour of something cold.
explanation.walkthrough: C, then SHERRY without its S.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherry is a small round stone fruit, typically red.

clue.text: Shrub Mary and George maybe covered with layer?

indicators.note: in a down entry, being covered means having something placed on top, so that word comes first

parts.note: a goose lays eggs, so it is a layer
Mary Berry is a famous British cookery writer and TV baking judge
George Bush, the US President

explanation.surface: Mary and George's child, perhaps, covered in a blanket; babies are said to come from under a gooseberry bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' warns that Mary and George are named examples: BERRY and BUSH. 'Layer' is not a stratum but something that lays, here GOOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A gooseberry bush is the thorny shrub that bears gooseberries, and also where children are jokingly told babies are found.

clue.text: Jack turned on one supporter at top of column

indicators.note: in an across entry, sitting on something means coming after it

parts.note: a means one

indicators.note: a word turned round is read back to front

parts.note: jack and salt are both slang for a sailor

explanation.surface: Jack turns to someone who props up the top of a column, like a building worker.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition hides an anatomy fact: the spinal column's top vertebra, which holds up the skull, is called the atlas.
explanation.definitionFit: The atlas is the first neck vertebra, supporting the head at the top of the spine, named after the Titan who held up the heavens.

clue.text: Rock destroyed remote locations lacking cover

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken apart, so its letters are rebuilt in another order
without its cover a word loses its outermost letters at both ends

parts.note: taken as written
sites are locations

explanation.surface: Rock bands destroying gigs in remote spots with no shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: REMOTE rearranged, then SITES stripped of its outer S's.
explanation.definitionFit: A meteorite is a rock from space that has survived falling to Earth.

clue.text: Come across smallest pig eating in ring

indicators.note: something eating takes food inside itself, so the little pig surrounds the next word

parts.note: the runt is the smallest of a litter
taken as written
O is shaped like a ring

explanation.surface: Coming across the smallest pig of the litter feeding in a ring.
explanation.definitionFit: To run into someone is to meet them by chance, an idiom for encountering.

clue.text: Person handling notes more like a country singer?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who deals with money at a bank or shop counter
second meaning, playful: a comparative adjective, as if 'cashy' meant like Johnny Cash

explanation.walkthrough: 'Notes' suggests music, which the country singer reinforces; they are banknotes. Johnny Cash was the American country singer, and the question mark licenses the invented comparative.
explanation.definitionFit: A cashier takes and pays out money, handling banknotes as a job, while the comparative reading is the setter's invented sense.

clue.text: Adage Rod composed in book fit for composting

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go inside the book

parts.note: the Bible is the book

indicators.note: to compose is to arrange, so the letters are set out in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An adage that someone called Rod wrote in a book about compost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' fits the writing picture and also hints at compost, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Something biodegradable can be broken down by bacteria, which is exactly what makes material suitable for the compost heap.

clue.text: Toby unwrapped hearing thing

indicators.note: removing the wrapping takes off the outside letters, leaving just the middle ones

parts.note: the inner letters of Toby
a court hearing or sitting is a session

explanation.surface: A Toby jug unwrapped, a much-heard-of thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' suggests the ear; here it is a sitting of a court.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a thing about something is informal for being fixated on it, which is what an obsession is.

clue.text: Learners cycling naked in streets facing each another

indicators.note: the shifted word sits between the two copies of the street abbreviation
two things facing each other point opposite ways, so the second copy is turned round
letters going round a cycle move from the front to the back of the word

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
nude means naked
a second street abbreviation

explanation.surface: Students cycling naked through the streets, a rag-week stunt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' paints bicycles but is the rotation signal: the first letter moves to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Students are people who are learning, at school or university.

clue.text: Poet Stephen welcoming American hit Lingerie

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so the poet's name wraps the next word

parts.note: Stephen Spender was an English poet
US for American
to belt is to hit hard

explanation.surface: A poet welcoming an American hit called Lingerie, a hit song or show.
explanation.walkthrough: SPENDER takes in US: S(US)PENDER, then BELT.
explanation.definitionFit: A suspender belt is women's underwear, a band with straps that hold up stockings.

clue.text: People sort of supporting Glen actively

indicators.note: in a down entry, a supporter sits underneath, so that piece comes last
letters that are active move about, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the suffix -ish means sort of, as in 'greenish'

explanation.surface: People who keenly support someone called Glen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporting' looks like cheering a person but is a placement instruction: in a down entry the supporter goes underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: The English are a people, the nation of England, and the word serves as a plural noun.

clue.text: Widow bet on event? On the contrary

indicators.note: this reverses the order the clue implies, so the event comes on top of the bet instead

parts.note: a do is a party or social event
a wager is a bet

explanation.surface: A widow placing a bet on a sporting event.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'bet on event' would put the bet above the event; 'On the contrary' flips that order.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowager is a widow holding a title or property from her late husband, as in dowager duchess.

clue.text: Mischief-makers infiltrated by the Spanish forces

indicators.note: whatever infiltrates a group gets inside it, so the article goes within

parts.note: imps are mischievous little sprites
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Troublemakers infiltrated by Spanish armed forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forces' looks like a military noun, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel someone is to drive or compel them, so impels works as a verb meaning forces.

clue.text: Equine character of Aesop flies around

parts.note: Aesop was Greek, and mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet

indicators.note: turned around, the insects' word is read from the back

parts.note: gnats are small flies

explanation.surface: A horse character from Aesop's fables with flies buzzing round it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a figure in a fable; it is a letter of Aesop's Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A mustang is a wild horse of the American West, and equine as a noun means a member of the horse family.

clue.text: Ambushed far west of city with papers

indicators.note: in an across entry, west is the left, so that piece comes first

parts.note: way means far, as in 'way off'
LA is Los Angeles
ID is identity papers

explanation.surface: Someone ambushed far to the west of a city while carrying documents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' looks like newspapers; it means identity documents.
explanation.definitionFit: To waylay someone is to lie in wait and stop or attack them on their way.

clue.text: One replaced by bishop in a 1760-yard walk

indicators.note: one thing replaced by another is swapped out for it, letter for letter

parts.note: taken as written
a mile is 1760 yards
I is the Roman numeral for one
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop taking a mile-long stroll in place of someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: A MILE has its I swapped for B.
explanation.definitionFit: An amble is a leisurely, easy-paced stroll.

clue.text: Wickedness of six stopping in lodge naughtily

indicators.note: something stopping a gap plugs it from inside, so the number sits within
naughty letters misbehave and get out of order

parts.note: taken as written
VI is six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Wickedness of six people misbehaving in a lodge, such as a Masonic one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link word but belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Evildoing is wicked behaviour, the deeds of an evildoer.

clue.text: You're texted by Nick about living in town?

parts.note: text-speak for you're

indicators.note: turned about, the verb for nick is read backwards

parts.note: to nick is to arrest or nab

explanation.surface: A text from Nick asking whether you are living in town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a name but is a verb meaning catch.
explanation.definitionFit: Urban describes city life; the question mark admits that a phrase like living in town only stands in for the adjective.

clue.text: Quickly downed five in Le Café, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a spoken sound, so the French word is matched by its pronunciation

parts.note: cinq is French for five, pronounced like the English word

explanation.surface: Five drinks downed fast at a French café.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Le Café' signals French.
explanation.definitionFit: To sink a pint is to drink it quickly, and the past tense means downed fast.

clue.text: Severity of exploit overwhelming first couple of sherpas

indicators.note: to overwhelm is to engulf completely, so the verb wraps around the kept letters

parts.note: to harness something is to exploit it

indicators.note: only the opening two letters of the following word are used

parts.note: the first two letters of sherpas

explanation.surface: The harshness of exploiting the Himalayan sherpas who carry loads for climbers.
explanation.walkthrough: Sherpas are Himalayan mountain guides and porters, which is why exploiting them is a harsh picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Harshness is the quality of being severe, cruel or rough.
